newsitem.title: LUXEMBOURG: Environment Council ends short on substance.
newsitem.headline: Environment Council ends short on substance.

text.p: Environment Ministers discussed a series of issues ranging from leg-hold traps to climate change on Tuesday but took no decisions on any substantive legal texts.

The set-piece of the day proved to be an unusually revealing open session on member states' initial reactions to the European Commission's Auto/Oil proposals, COM(96)248, which received a mixed response from ministers.
Ministers also reached conclusions on the EU's position for November's Buenos Aires meeting of the parties to the convention on biodiversity.
They also held an orientation debate on the European Commission's proposal to review the fifth framework action programme for the environment, COM(95)647.
A common position by the December Council remains one of the presidency's main environment aims, Environment Minister Brendan Howlin said after the meeting.
Ministers also discussed Ireland's second common position target, the Commission proposal to modify Directive 90/219 on the contained use of genetically modified organisms (GMOs).

"The Council discussions focused in particular on key provisions relating to risk assessment, classification of contained use and identification of appropriate containment levels and administrative procedures," Howlin said.

The proposal suggests changing the scope of Directive 90/219, altering the committee procedures for technical amendment, changing the risk categorisation and the administrative procedures and further specifying required containment and control measures.
It would abolish the different regulatory treatment for research laboratories and industrial ones.
Ministers also tackled questions related to the Commission's proposal for a review of the Community strategy for waste management, COM(96)399.

Howlin said detailed further work for an eventual draft resolution was needed on what to do about transboundary waste for incineration, application of the Commission's idea of producer responsibility for waste and the need for waste minimisation measures.

Another orientation debate took place on the Commission's proposal COM(94)612 for changes to the drinking water Directive 80/778. Member states generally accepted the proposals to cut allowed lead content to bring it into line with World Health Organisation standards although they differed on who should pay, Howlin told the post-Council news conference.
The question of allowed limits of individual and accumulated pesticides also arose, Howlin said.
"I think there is emerging consensus that we have to look not only at the individual limit values but (also) to revisit the cumulative effects of cocktails or baskets of pesticides," he said.
Ministers also discussed briefly their follow-up to June's conference on climate change and prepared the EU position for protocol negotiations.
Among the other items, environment ministers also heard a report on progress with leg-hold trap talks (see BC-ENVIRONMENT-FUR, moved earlier).
